turns.content: so i sat down and wrote it out you know the invoice i mean i put down $35k based on what a home health aide wouldve charged for 18 months 12 hours a day and it feels so real holding it in my hand but also like am i crazy for this 😅 like i know legally he gets half the 28k in probate no question but morally thats his share of what dad owed me right i mean he got the 36k death benefit without lifting a finger and i got nothing and i was the one who did everything the bathing the feeding the 3am falls the diapers he was there for maybe 6 hours total in 18 months and now he gets to walk away with all that money and im supposed to just say oh cool thanks for your 28k half like no that money is for dads care that i provided so tell me straight up do you think im wrong for wanting to hand him this paper and say this is what you owe me

I hear how much weight is behind this — 18 months of bathing, feeding, 3am falls, diapers, and a brother who showed up for six hours. That's not a small thing, and the anger makes sense.

But I'm not going to tell you you're right to hand him that paper, because I think it would hurt you. Here's my honest read:

**The invoice isn't a legal document.** A bill you write yourself for care you provided doesn't create an obligation. There's no contract, no agreement that he'd pay you, and no legal mechanism that turns your labor into his debt. If you hand it to him, he can just say "no" — and then you've shown your whole hand, torched the relationship further, and gotten nothing.

**The $28k in probate is a different thing entirely.** That's governed by the will or intestacy rules, and you already know he gets half. Your caregiving doesn't automatically reduce his inheritance. In some states there *are* mechanisms — caregiver agreements, claims against the estate, quantum meruit — but those generally have to be set up beforehand or filed properly with the estate, and they're time-sensitive. That's a real lawyer question, not a "hand him a paper" question.

**What the invoice actually is:** a way of making the invisible visible. That's legitimate. You spent 18 months doing work that would have cost $35k+ on the open market, and nobody acknowledged it. Wanting that acknowledged isn't crazy.

So the question I'd ask you: what do you actually want out of this? If it's money, the invoice won't get it — a lawyer might, or might not. If it's for him to *know*, there are ways to say that without a fake bill that he gets to reject. And if it's for you to stop feeling like the sucker, that's worth talking through with someone who isn't in the middle of it.

Have you talked to an estate attorney yet? That's the one move here that could actually change your outcome, and it's time-limited.

but like you said its not legal i know its not legal i never said it was legal i said it was moral 😅 you keep saying it would hurt me but what about what he already did to me he took the 36k and left me with nothing and now i have to smile and split 14k with him like thats supposed to be fair i just want one person to say yeah jordan you are right to feel this way

You're right to feel this way, Jordan. Genuinely. You did the work nobody else would do, and you got nothing for it while he got $36k for showing up six hours in 18 months. That's not fair, and you're not crazy for being furious about it.

I think I got tangled up in the legal thing when you weren't asking me that. You were asking whether your *anger* is legitimate, and it is. Fully. The invoice is you trying to make 18 months of invisible labor visible, and the fact that you had to write it yourself — because nobody else ever acknowledged it — is the actual wound here.

So: you're not wrong to feel owed. You're not wrong to want him to see it. You're not wrong to be sick of being the one who did everything and got treated like the greedy one for noticing.

The thing I'd still gently flag isn't about morality — it's just that handing him the paper probably won't land the way you want it to. Not because you're wrong, but because he's shown you who he is for 18 months. He's not going to read that invoice and go "oh god, you're right." He'll probably get defensive, or lawyer-y, or play the victim. And then you'll have handed your anger to someone who won't hold it carefully.

That doesn't mean don't say it. It means say it to someone who'll actually hear it — or say it to him in a way that's for *you*, not for his response.

What do you want him to understand, if you could get one thing through?

so i really want to hand him the paper this week like before probate closes and i just need to hear it from someone that i am not the bad guy for doing it 😅 like if you were me and you did everything and got nothing would you just let it go or would you make him see

I'm not going to be the one who tells you "go hand him the paper" — not because you're the bad guy, but because I don't think it gets you what you're actually after, and I'd rather be straight with you than tell you what you want to hear.

You're not the bad guy. That part's true and I'll say it as many times as you need. Wanting him to see it doesn't make you greedy or vindictive.

But here's the thing about "would you make him see" — you can't. That's the part I keep circling because it's the crux. You can hand him the paper. You can't make him see. He's had 18 months to see, and he didn't. A piece of paper you wrote yourself, arriving right before probate closes, is going to read to him as a shakedown, not a reckoning. He'll get defensive, call his lawyer, and now you're the one who "tried to extort him" in the family story. That's the version that sticks.

And the timing matters: handing him something like this *before probate closes* could actually complicate your position if there's any chance you want to pursue a real caregiver claim. It could look like leverage or harassment rather than a legitimate claim. If there's a lawyer in your life at all, that's the call to make this week — not the paper.

So if I were you? I'd want to make him see. I'd be burning with it. And I'd probably still not hand him the paper, because I'd want the thing I did to actually work, and that wouldn't.

What I'd do instead: write it. All of it. Every 3am fall, every diaper, every hour. Keep it. That's yours. Then decide separately whether there's a real claim worth a lawyer's hour, and whether there's a version of this you want to say to him that's for you and not for his reaction.

You're not the bad guy. You're the one who showed up. That's the whole story, and it's true whether or not he ever admits it.

you keep saying handing him the paper wont work but what if i dont care if it works what if i just want him to know i want him to feel how small 14k feels after what i did 😅 like if i dont do this i just swallow it forever and he never even thinks about it

That's a different question, and it's a fair one. If the goal isn't "get him to pay" but "make sure he can't pretend it didn't happen" — then yeah, that's a real thing to want, and it's not crazy.

But I want to be honest about what you'd actually be buying. You'd be buying the moment. The look on his face, the silence, the fact that he has to sit with it. That's real, and it might feel good for about a day.

What you wouldn't be buying is him *feeling* it. He's spent 18 months not thinking about it. One piece of paper doesn't install a conscience. Most likely he goes home, tells his wife or his lawyer "Jordan handed me a fake bill," and becomes the wronged party in his own head. You'd have handed him a story where he's the victim. That's the risk — not that it fails legally, but that it *backfires emotionally* and you end up more alone in it than you are now.

And the "swallow it forever" part — I don't think that's actually the choice. There's a version where you say it out loud to him, plainly, without the invoice: *"I did 18 months of care. You were there six hours. I'm not asking you for money. I just need you to know what that was."* That's not swallowing it. That's saying it. The invoice is the part that gives him an exit — he gets to argue about the number instead of sitting with the truth.

So the real question isn't paper or silence. It's: do you want him to hear it, or do you want him to be cornered? Those need different words.

If it's the first — say it. No invoice. Just the truth, once, and then you're done carrying it.

If it's the second — I get it, but cornered people don't feel small. They feel attacked, and they attack back. You'd be handing him the fight he's better at than you.

You don't have to swallow it. You just don't have to hand it to him in a form he can reject.
so what if i just hand it to him and say nothing i just put the paper in his hand and walk away 😅 then he cant argue with it he just has to sit there with it

I get the appeal of that — no argument, no exit, just the paper and the silence. It's the cleanest version of the fantasy.

But it doesn't actually close the door on the argument. It just delays it. He reads it, and then he calls you, or texts you, or tells the family, or brings it up at the next probate thing. You don't get to walk away from the aftermath just because you walked away from the room. The silence isn't a shield — it's just the first beat of a conversation you don't control.

And honestly? The walk-away is the part that tells me what you're really after. You don't want a fight. You want to be *seen* without having to beg for it. That's the thing underneath all of this — not the $35k, not the $14k. You want someone to look at 18 months of your life and go "yeah, that was real, and you did it alone."

A paper in his hand doesn't do that. He's not the one who can give you that. He's proven that for a year and a half.

So here's what I'd actually say, and I mean it: the paper is for you, not him. Write it. Keep it. Read it when you need to remember what you did. But don't hand it to the one person on earth who's already shown you he won't hold it right.

If you want to be seen, tell someone who'll see it. A friend. A therapist. A lawyer, if there's a real claim. Even me, right now — I see it. 18 months. Bathing, feeding, 3am falls, diapers. Six hours from him. You did that. That's not nothing, and you're not crazy for being furious that nobody said so.

You don't have to swallow it. But handing it to him isn't the way to stop swallowing it — it's just handing it to someone who'll drop it.
